source_document.body:
Deposco ’s Q3 2026 Commerce Signal report found that parcel carrier rates fell 3.3% from the second quarter, but what companies actually paid per package fell only 0.6%. Heavier packages, faster shipping services, and more residential deliveries ate into those savings.
What’s Related
The report draws on shipping, sales, and inventory activity flowing through Deposco’s software . The company says its platform serves more than 4,900 supply chain operators, accounting for over $84 billion in annual merchandise sales and 485 million orders.
“Rates came down, but operators didn’t feel it. That’s the story of the quarter,” said Eric Lemus, vice president of strategy and data analytics at Deposco.
“Every margin conversation we’re having right now comes back to what actually shipped. That’s where the money went and where operators should focus.”
RELATED: USPS Plans Peak Rate Hikes for Heavy, Long-Distance Packages | Peak Season Outlook Brightens as 52% Expect More Freight Activity
Why there is so little savings
Deposco compared what it would cost to ship the same mix of packages in both quarters with what companies actually paid. Rates fell, but companies shipped heavier packages and used more expensive delivery services, leaving them with little savings.
That distinction helps explain the quarter’s results. Lower rates offered some relief, but changes in package weight, delivery speed, and destination ate into the savings. The report also cited regional carriers raising fees.
Costs remained higher than a year earlier. Deposco reported that actual parcel costs per package were up 6.9% year over year, despite the small quarterly decline.
Orders grew as inventory caught up
Order growth stood at 5.3% year over year at the quarter’s close, while gross merchandise value, the dollar value of goods sold, grew 11.7%. Average order value increased 4.1%.
Inventory also rose late in the quarter. Median days of inventory on hand reached 93, up from 88 in mid-September and level with the same period last year. The increase closed a year-over-year inventory gap during the final three weeks of September.
The findings reflect activity among Deposco customers, not the entire shipping market. Deposco says the data is aggregated and anonymized, and its figures are approximate.
Expect a more expensive peak season
Deposco expects per-package costs to rise during the holiday shipping season , pointing to peak surcharges and renewed pressure from fuel prices.
The company also revisited its July prediction that parcel inflation would keep climbing during the third quarter. Rates instead declined, and Deposco said the new report explains the missed forecast and changes to its methods.
“Shipping costs cooled during Q3. But get ready for an expensive peak season,” the report stated.
